newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Australia-Indonesia ties strong despite race row.
newsitem.headline: Australia-Indonesia ties strong despite race row.

text.p: Canberra's ties with Indonesia continue to grow strongly despite the negative impact in Asia of an Australian race row, statistics released on Friday by the Australian embassy in Jakarta showed.

Independent legislator Pauline Hanson sparked a bitter race debate in Australia after she called for cuts to Asian immigration and attacked welfare for native Aborigines in her maiden parliamentary speech last September.

The figures were released after news this week that Australia had set up a special diplomatic unit to combat the country's negative image in Asia, fuelled by Hanson's speech and her rising prominence.
That move followed a secret campaign by Australia's foreign affairs department to discredit Hanson in the region.
"Bearing in mind the impact of the Hanson issue in the region, Indonesians are certainly not being discouraged from going to Australia," an Australian embassy spokesman said in a statement.

Embassy figures for 1996-97 showed that the issuing of all visitor visas increased by 11.6 percent over the previous 12 months, while business visas increased by 21 percent and education visas rose by 20 percent over the previous year.
The statement said for the month of July 1997, student visas had increased by 37 percent compared with July 1996, while visitor visas increased by 29 percent.
It said the number of student visas issued in July 1997 was the highest recorded for any month.
An embassy official said there were now more than 16,000 Indonesians studying in Australia and this made it the number one destination for Indonesians studying abroad, surpassing the United States.
"Incidentally, the number of flights both ways between Australia and Indonesia has now almost tripled since 1992. They number about 150 per week," the statement said.
